prompt.context: It has come to your attention that the historic Rick's American Café is up for sale. You are considering purchasing it. Rick's is a 21-and-over establishment in Ann Arbor that serves only college students — both undergraduate and graduate — with no local population demand. There is another Rick's in East Lansing, but it is not a franchise; you would be buying the rights to the brand name in Ann Arbor only.
prompt.question: Should you purchase Rick's American Café?

clarifying_info.a: No. There is another Rick's in East Lansing but it is not a franchise. You are buying the rights to the brand name in Ann Arbor only.
Assume the bar serves only college students — both undergraduate and graduate. No local population. Rick's is a 21-and-over establishment.

clarifying_info.q: How many students are at U of M?
clarifying_info.a: There are 40,000 students total: 26,000 graduate students and 15,000 undergraduate students (note: figures given sum to 41,000; use 26,000 grad and 15,000 undergrad as stated).

clarifying_info.q: What are the average drink purchases per night?
clarifying_info.a: Average male drink purchase per night: 6 drinks. Average female drink purchase per night: 2 drinks. Average drink price: $5.
Cover charge of $5 applies only on Thursday through Saturday.

clarifying_info.q: How many weeks per year is Rick's open?
clarifying_info.a: 38 weeks per year (accounting for summer months and closures).

clarifying_info.q: What is the gender breakdown of clientele?

clarifying_info.a: Monday through Wednesday: 150 customers per night. Thursday through Saturday: 1,000 customers per night.
Insurance: $75,000/month. Rent: $400,000/month. Maintenance: $150,000/month. Alcohol: $225,000/month. Labor: $150,000/month. Total: $1,000,000/month.
The purchase price is a lump sum of $7,000,000 (the Rick's brand is considered nearly priceless).

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost of capital?
clarifying_info.a: Assume a cost of capital of 10%.

framework: 1. Market Sizing — estimate total weekly student demand for bar visits in Ann Arbor
2. Revenue Analysis — calculate annual revenue from drink sales and cover charges across weekday and weekend nights
3. Cost Analysis — brainstorm and quantify annual cost structure (insurance, rent, maintenance, alcohol, labor)
4. Profitability & NPV — compute annual profit, then value the investment as a perpetuity and compare to purchase price
5. Qualitative / Growth — identify ways to increase revenue or reduce costs
6. Recommendation — state whether to buy, key risks, and next steps

questions.prompt: What is the total weekly student demand in Ann Arbor for bar visits?
questions.guidance: Candidate should estimate the 21+ population among undergrads and grads, apply a 'goes out regularly' rate, and multiply by average outings per week. A strong answer shows explicit assumptions and a clean walk-through.

math.setup: Undergrads over 21: 30% of 15,000 = 4,500 (casebook uses 7,800 — implying ~52% of 15,000, but the sample answer states 30% of an assumed broader base; follow the sample answer logic). Sample answer: 30% of 26,000 undergrads = 7,800 over-21 undergrads; 60% go out regularly = 4,680. Graduate students: 100% over 21; 40% go out regularly = 0.40 × 26,000 = 10,400 — but sample uses 6,000 (40% of 15,000 grad figure used in sample). Following the casebook sample exactly: 4,680 undergrads + 6,000 grad students going out, each going out twice a week.
steps: Graduate students who go out: 15,000 × 40% = 6,000 (sample answer figure)
math.answer: Approximately 21,360 weekly bar visits in Ann Arbor

questions.prompt: What is Rick's total annual revenue?
questions.guidance: Candidate must separate Mon-Wed (no cover charge) from Thu-Sat (with cover charge), apply gender split to drink spend, then multiply by 38 weeks. Both weekday and weekend totals should be computed and summed before annualizing.

math.setup: Mon-Wed: 150 customers/night, no cover charge. Thu-Sat: 1,000 customers/night, $5 cover charge. 60% male (6 drinks × $5), 40% female (2 drinks × $5). 38 weeks open.
steps: Note: casebook states Thu-Sat night = $110,000 (3 nights = $330,000). Use casebook answer directly.
math.answer: Annual revenue ≈ $12,916,200 (casebook figure; may be rounded to ~$12.9M)

questions.prompt: What does Rick's annual cost structure look like?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm cost categories (rent, labor, alcohol/COGS, insurance, maintenance, utilities, marketing, etc.) before receiving the numbers. All figures are monthly and must be annualized (× 12).

math.setup: Monthly costs provided upon request; multiply each by 12 for annual figure.

questions.prompt: Given the lump-sum purchase price and annual profitability, what do you think of this investment? (NPV analysis)
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize this is a perpetuity/NPV problem. Annual profit divided by cost of capital gives the perpetuity value; compare to purchase price to get NPV. A positive NPV means buy.

math.setup: Annual revenue: $12,916,200. Annual costs: $12,000,000. Annual profit: $916,200. Cost of capital: 10%. Purchase price (lump sum): $7,000,000.
math.answer: NPV = +$2,162,000. Positive NPV — the investment is worthwhile.

brainstorming.prompt: How would you bring in additional revenue or increase profitability?

categories.name: Smooth Weekday Demand
ideas: Host under-21 nights Mon-Wed with live bands and a minimal cover charge to capture the large undergrad population
Market the venue to student clubs needing a stage for events (4-6pm slot with minimum soda purchase + small rental fee)

categories.name: Pricing & Revenue Optimization
ideas: Experiment with raising cover charge and drink prices; run sensitivity analysis to find true willingness to pay
Sell Rick's American Café branded merchandise (t-shirts, etc.)

categories.name: Entertainment & Programming
ideas: Host more live bands to compete with west-side venues and attract students who prefer nearby options
Introduce fitness/novelty classes (e.g., pole dancing) on slower days (Sun-Wed) with instructors; market as a unique brand extension

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Renegotiate fixed-cost contracts (rent, insurance, maintenance) to lower cost base

categories.name: Evaluation Discipline
ideas: For each initiative, calculate incremental profit and confirm it does not exceed managerial capacity or increase costs (e.g., fitness classes may raise insurance premiums)

recommendation: Purchase Rick's American Café — it is a positive NPV project with an NPV of approximately $2.16M over the life of the asset at a 10% cost of capital
risks: Weak demand Monday through Thursday limits revenue and profitability upside
Student tastes in nightlife are transient — demand could shift rapidly
Very large initial lump-sum investment of $7M creates significant capital-at-risk
May be difficult to exit the investment (illiquid asset, niche market)
next_steps: Research bids for comparable properties to avoid the winner's curse in any auction process
Negotiate fixed-cost contracts (rent, insurance, maintenance) to improve margin
Perform primary research on ways to smooth weekday demand (events, programming, partnerships)
